title: Quadratic and cubic graphs from features
what_it_asks: You are given a quadratic or cubic, or a description of its features. You are asked to sketch it, read off intercepts and turning points, or describe a region with inequalities. Roots, the completed-square form and the sign of the leading coefficient fix the shape and position of the curve. You often then solve an inequality or use the discriminant to link the graph to an equation.
typical_structure: Usually two or three parts, with about seven marks in total. A part often moves from a short setup (complete the square, factorise, state a value) to a sketch, then to an inequality or a condition on a constant. Later parts sometimes say "hence" and expect you to reuse an earlier result. About a third of questions come with a diagram.
mark_pattern: The most typical part is M1 A1: a method step, then the correct result. Four-mark parts are often M1 A1 M1 A1. You find critical values first, then use them to choose the correct region. B1 M1 A1 appears when a stated value or shape earns an independent mark before the working. Sketch parts often use B1 B1 B1, with one mark each for shape, intercepts and turning point or end behaviour. M1 dM1 A1 appears when a second step depends on the first, such as forming the discriminant and then solving for a constant. A show-that part ends with a starred or cso accuracy mark.

where_marks_leak.text: Many students give the final answer to the wrong number of significant figures or decimal places, or round too early. The final A1 is lost even though the method was right.

This is a common slip: you forget to take out the $x^2$ coefficient, halve the wrong number or get the constant wrong. The M1 for the form is lost, and the A1 and any dM1 that use the turning point go with it.
A numerical slip in a correct method is often made when finding roots or intercepts. The A1 is lost, and later accuracy marks may be lost unless follow-through applies.
You read $a$, $b$ and $c$ before moving everything to one side to equal zero. The M1 for the discriminant is lost, and the dependent marks for the condition and the range of the constant go too.
Many students factorise with the wrong signs, so the roots have the wrong sign. The M1 may be lost, and the sketch intercepts and the inequality regions then fail their A1 or B1 marks.

write_to_earn: Write the completed-square form or the factorised form as its own line before you read off any feature.
On a sketch, label every intercept with its coordinates and mark the turning point, because each feature can carry its own B1.
For an inequality, write the critical values first, then sketch the curve and state the region in inequality notation.
For a discriminant condition, rearrange to equal zero first, then write $b^2-4ac$ with your values substituted.
In a show-that part, write the step just before the printed result, then the printed result.
check_before_you_leave: Inside or outside region chosen correctly
